self.text: Which best describes your work right now?

options.label: I lead or manage a team
I run my own business or freelance

team.text: How many people are in the team you're thinking about?

self.text: How do you usually feel on a Sunday evening, thinking about the week ahead?

options.label: Ready. I'm quietly looking forward to it
Fine. A bit of admin in my head, nothing heavy
A low hum of dread I can't quite shake
Heavy. It takes over my evening

team.text: How does your team usually seem at the start of the week?

options.label: Energised. People arrive with ideas and momentum
Steady. A slow start, then into the flow
Flat. Quiet, low energy and slow to get going
Strained. Tense, irritable or already firefighting

self.text: When you get home or close the laptop, how much of you is left?

options.label: Plenty. I have energy for the people and things I love
Enough. A little tired, but present

team.text: By the end of the week, what do you usually notice?

options.label: Still engaged. Good humour and ideas in the room
Tired but steady. Winding down at a normal pace
Drained. Short replies and mistakes creeping in
Running on empty. Snapping, sick days or people checking out

self.text: Outside working hours, how easily can you switch off from work?

team.text: How often do you see work messages from your team outside working hours?

options.label: Rarely. Evenings and weekends stay quiet
Now and then, usually before a deadline
Most evenings, from a few people
Constantly, from most of the team

self.text: Looking back over the last month, how do you feel about what you've achieved?

options.label: Proud. I can see the good work I've done
Unsure. Busy, but it's hard to see progress
Frustrated. Effort isn't turning into results

team.text: When your team finishes a piece of work, what usually happens?

options.label: We notice the progress and celebrate it
Big wins get noticed, smaller ones less so
We ship it and move straight on to the next thing
It's hard to point to finished work. Effort doesn't seem to turn into results

enablerTips.clarity: Name the one outcome that matters most this week and let it decide what waits.
enablerTips.autonomy: Autonomy is one of the strongest predictors of satisfaction at work. Agree the outcome, then hand over the how.
enablerTips.focus: Protect one 90-minute block a day, notifications off, and treat it like a meeting.
enablerTips.recovery: Recovery works best when it's planned. Put the breaks in the calendar before the work fills it.
enablerTips.trust: Trust grows through small, kept promises. Do what you said, when you said, and say it out loud.
enablerTips.appreciation: Specific beats generic: name what someone did and the difference it made.
enablerTips.growth: Pick one skill to stretch this quarter and ask for one piece of feedback on it each month.
enablerTips.leadership: Ask for, or offer, one explicit commitment: what support looks like when things get hard.
enablerTips.flexibility: Agree a few core hours together, then give real freedom around them.
enablerTips.mission: Reconnect to who the work is for. One real story from a customer or colleague goes a long way.
enablerTips.workload: List what's on the plate and what could come off. Sustainable pace is a team decision, not a personal failing.
enablerTips.environment: Light, movement and quiet are levers. Change one thing about where the work happens this week.

self.summary: You have energy in the tank and you know why the work matters. This is the state most people are chasing: work that feels purposeful without draining you dry.
self.detail: Flow is valuable and it can be fragile. It usually rests on a handful of conditions, like a protected rhythm, people you trust and a clear sense of purpose. When those slip, energy is often the first thing to go. The opportunity is to understand what's keeping you here, so you can protect it on purpose and help others find it too.
self.outcome: Use your result to notice what your best weeks have in common, and build those conditions into the weeks that aren't.

team.summary: Your team has energy and a shared sense of why the work matters. People are bringing their best and getting something back from it.
team.detail: Teams in Flow are a real asset, and they are easy to take for granted. Flow tends to rest on a few conditions: a sustainable rhythm, trust and a clear purpose. Growth, deadlines or a change in leadership can quietly erode them. The opportunity is to name what's working, so you can protect it as the team changes.
team.outcome: Use your result to turn what's working into shared habits the team can keep when pressure rises.

exercises.title: Best-week blueprint
exercises.self: Think back to your two best working weeks this year. Write down what was true in both: how you started the day, who you spent time with, what you said no to. Circle the three conditions that mattered most and put one of them in next week's calendar.
exercises.team: In your next team meeting, ask everyone to write down what was true in the team's best week this year. Cluster the answers and agree on three conditions you'll protect as a team.

exercises.title: Recover before you need it
exercises.self: Choose one restoring practice, like a silent meal, a walk without your phone or two minutes of slow breathing, and do it once a week while things are going well. Recovery is easier to build when you're not depleted.
exercises.team: Pick one restoring ritual the whole team can share, like a walking meeting or a no-meetings Friday afternoon. Trial it for a month while energy is high.

exercises.title: Team Weather check-in
exercises.self: Ask one colleague, "What's your weather like this week?" and share yours. Sunny, changeable, foggy, stormy. Moods spread through teams, so paying attention to the people around you helps protect the climate you're in.
exercises.team: Open your next meeting with a one-word weather report from everyone: sunny, changeable, foggy or stormy. No fixing, just listening. Over time it becomes an early-warning system for the team.

sprinter.name: Sprinter
sprinter.tagline: Moving fast, unsure what it's for

self.summary: You have energy and you're getting things done, but the why feels thin. The days are full and the sense of direction or difference you're making isn't keeping up.
self.detail: Sprinters often look fine from the outside, and they're productive and capable. The research on burnout and engagement treats energy and meaning as separate dimensions, and when meaning stays low for long enough, energy tends to follow it down. The good news is that meaning responds to small, regular reconnection: seeing who your work helps, how it fits together and what you care about.
self.outcome: Use your result to reconnect your effort to a purpose, before speed turns into drift.

team.summary: Your team has energy and delivers, but the shared why feels thin. There's a lot of motion, and less sense of direction or of the difference the work makes.
team.detail: Sprinter teams often hit their numbers while quietly losing their sense of purpose. Energy without meaning is hard to sustain, and over time it can show up as disengagement, cynicism or people leaving for somewhere that feels more purposeful. Meaning grows when people see how their work fits together, who it helps and what the team is building towards.
team.outcome: Use your result to reconnect the team's effort to a shared purpose people can feel.

exercises.title: Trace the thread
exercises.self: Pick one task on today's list and ask "Who does this help, and how?" Then ask it again of your answer, three times. Write down where the thread ends up. That's the purpose behind the task.
exercises.team: In your next stand-up, ask each person to name one piece of work from the week and who it helped. Keep a running list where the team can see it.

exercises.title: Find your superpower
exercises.self: Write about a recent moment at work when you felt most like yourself. What were you doing? What strength were you using? Look for one place to use that strength on purpose this week.
exercises.team: Go round the team: each person shares a moment they felt most like themselves at work and the strength they were using. Notice where those strengths could be used more.

exercises.title: Intention before action
exercises.self: Before you open your inbox, set one intention for the day that names why rather than what. For example: "Today I'm working so the new starters feel welcome." Come back to it at lunch.
exercises.team: Start the week with a one-line headline for the team that answers "Why does this week's work matter?" Revisit it on Friday.

self.summary: You care about your work and you know why it matters, but your energy is running low. The commitment is there and the tank is close to empty.
self.detail: Embers are often the people others rely on most. Caring deeply can make it hard to stop, and in the research, high demands without enough recovery are one of the clearest paths to exhaustion. Your meaning is a real strength. The priority now is restoring energy, so your commitment has something to run on.
self.outcome: Use your result to rebuild your energy with small, daily recovery habits, without losing what you care about.

team.summary: Your team cares about the work and knows why it matters, but energy is running low. Commitment is high and reserves are thin.
team.detail: Ember teams are often mission-driven teams carrying a lot. Caring deeply can make it hard to slow down, and high demands without enough recovery are one of the clearest paths to burnout in the research. Shared purpose is a real strength. The priority now is restoring energy and making recovery a shared norm rather than a private struggle.
team.outcome: Use your result to make recovery part of how the team works, so its commitment stays sustainable.

exercises.title: Abdominal breathing
exercises.self: Place one hand on your chest and the other on your belly. Breathe in through your nose so your belly, not your chest, rises. Exhale slowly, a little longer than the in-breath. Repeat for two minutes.
exercises.team: Open your next meeting with one minute of slow breathing together: in through the nose, longer out-breath. It takes sixty seconds and changes the tone of the room.

exercises.title: A shutdown ritual
exercises.self: At the end of each workday, write down tomorrow's top three, close every tab and say (out loud if you like) "Done for today." Psychologically detaching from work is one of the strongest predictors of recovery.
exercises.team: Agree a team switch-off norm, such as no messages after 6pm or delayed-send by default, and have leaders model it first.

exercises.title: The 80% question
exercises.self: Ask yourself: "If I only had 80% of my energy for the next month, what would I protect, and what would I let go?" Write both lists. Pick one thing from the let-go list to drop this week.
exercises.team: Run a 'stop doing' session: everyone lists work that costs energy and adds little. Agree one thing the team will stop, pause or simplify this month.

self.summary: Energy is low and the sense of why is hard to find right now. Work may feel heavy, flat or hard to see through.
self.detail: Fog is common, and it's a signal rather than a verdict. It often builds slowly, as demands outpace recovery and connection to purpose fades. The way out usually starts small: steadying your energy first, then reconnecting with people and with one thing that matters to you. You don't have to clear all of it at once.
self.outcome: Use your result to take one small step for your energy and one for your connection, and notice what shifts.

team.summary: Energy is low across the team and the shared why is hard to find right now. Work may feel heavy, flat or hard to see through.
team.detail: Team Fog is common, especially after long stretches of change, pressure or uncertainty. It's a signal rather than a verdict. Teams usually come out of it in small steps: steadying energy first, then reconnecting people to each other and to a purpose they believe in. It helps to hear from the whole team, so you're working from what people actually feel.
team.outcome: Use your result to start a conversation about where the team is, and agree one small step for energy and one for connection.

exercises.title: Muscle clench and release
exercises.self: Clench your fists and toes tightly for five seconds, then release and notice the relaxation. Repeat three times. Starting with the body is often easier than starting with the mind.
exercises.team: Try a one-minute clench-and-release together at the start of a meeting. It's a little silly, and that helps too.

exercises.title: One good thing
exercises.self: Each evening this week, write down one thing that went well at work and why it went well. Small counts. This simple practice has good evidence for lifting mood over time.
exercises.team: End the week with a two-minute wins round: each person names one thing that went well. Leaders go last.

exercises.title: Connect with others
exercises.self: Have a ten-minute conversation with one colleague that isn't about work. Ask what they're looking forward to. Connection is one of the quickest ways back to energy and meaning.
exercises.team: Pair people up for a ten-minute walk-and-talk with one prompt: "What's something you're looking forward to?" Rotate pairs weekly.

intro.self: Each of us has our own nervous system, and the people we work with form a collective one. Team Weather reads how that collective nervous system is holding up: how safe it feels, how moods travel and how well people recover together.
intro.team: Each of us has our own nervous system, and a team forms a collective one. Team Weather reads how your team's collective nervous system is holding up: how safe it feels, how moods travel and how well people recover together.

clear.name: Clear skies
clear.self: You feel you belong and it feels safe to speak up. That's a strong base. People in climates like this recover from setbacks faster.
clear.team: People feel they belong and it's safe to speak up. That's a strong base, and teams with climates like this recover from setbacks faster.

changeable.name: Changeable
changeable.self: Belonging and safety are there some of the time. The climate may shift with deadlines, meetings or who's in the room.
changeable.team: Belonging and safety are there some of the time. The climate may shift with deadlines, pressure or who's in the room.

overcast.name: Overcast
overcast.self: Belonging or safety feels low right now. That makes everything else harder, and it's one of the most worthwhile things to work on.
overcast.team: Belonging or safety feels low right now. That makes everything else harder, and it's one of the most worthwhile places for a team to start.

teamWeather.whyFive: These five elements come from decades of research into how groups feel, think and recover together. Our nervous systems are social: they constantly pick up cues from the people around us and adjust to them. Each element describes one way that happens at work, and together they shape whether a team can perform at its peak without burning out.

elements.name: Shared emotional tone
elements.text: How moods spread through the team, for better and worse.
elements.why: We automatically mirror the faces, voices and body language of the people around us. Research on teams shows one person's mood can ripple through a whole group and change how well it cooperates and decides.

elements.name: Shared safety
elements.text: Whether people can speak up, take risks and admit mistakes.
elements.why: The brain is always scanning for social threat. When people fear blame or embarrassment, the stress response kicks in and narrows thinking. Psychological safety is one of the strongest predictors of how well teams learn and perform.

elements.name: Attunement and airtime
elements.text: Whether people read each other well and everyone gets heard.
elements.why: Teams that read each other's signals and share airtime solve problems better than groups of individually brilliant people. Early brain research even suggests that people who are tuned in to each other start to show similar patterns of brain activity.

elements.name: Shared rhythm
elements.text: The rituals and pace that pull the team together.
elements.why: Doing things together in time, like moving, breathing, pausing or celebrating, builds trust and belonging. Predictable rhythms give the nervous system something to settle into, so energy goes into the work rather than staying on alert.

elements.name: Shared recovery and load
elements.text: How pressure is carried, and whether the team recovers together.
elements.why: Stress is contagious: watching a stressed colleague can raise your own stress response. Supportive people have the opposite effect. The brain treats them as shared resources, so the same challenge feels lighter when it's carried together.

leaders: An early-warning system for burnout and conflict, before they show up in sick days or resignations
Clearer thinking and better decisions under pressure
Faster recovery after setbacks, deadlines and change
A team people want to stay in
individuals: Less absorbing other people's stress without noticing
More confidence to speak up and ask for what you need
Energy left at the end of the day
Simple ways to reset yourself and your team when the weather turns

teamReport.name: Team Weather report
teamReport.line: Invite everyone on your team to complete an in-depth Team Weather Discovery and get a combined report: where individuals sit on the Team Archetypes, the five elements driving your Team's Weather, and a personalised practice plan. Individual answers stay confidential, with anonymised results used to provide insight into overall team dynamics.

support: If you've felt exhausted or low for more than a couple of weeks, please talk to someone: your GP, your Employee Assistance Programme if you have one, or Mind (mind.org.uk). If you need to talk right now, Samaritans are free to call on 116 123, day or night.
disclaimer: Workwell Discovery is a reflection tool. It isn't a clinical or psychometric assessment and it can't diagnose anything. The archetypes are in beta and are being reviewed with a neuroscience advisor.
